title: The Exorcist
synopsis: A movie-star mother in Georgetown, a small daughter who plays with a board, a priest who is losing his faith, and a long staircase outside a bedroom window.

nodes.text: Ninety-eight degrees in the shade at the dig above Mosul, and the workmen have stopped to watch you. The amulet is green stone, two inches, a head with a dog's snout on a body that is mostly wings. Nobody sifts this level expecting demons; it came up beside a lamp and a string of beads. You take your heart pills twice inside an hour and walk uphill to stand where the wind starts.

choices.consequence: You turn it over in your palm the way you would a foreign coin, and recognise the face, and your hands understand what that means before the rest of you does.
You label it, seal it, hand it to a student, and it rides in your chest cavity all the way to the airfield regardless.

nodes.text: Georgetown in October, and the house is a rental with good bones and a radiator that knocks at four in the morning. Regan's window has been swelling in its frame since the rain. There is a draft in her room and the thermostat insists the house is warm. You go up at two to check on her and find the curtain lifting with the sash shut, and your own breath visible over her bed.

choices.consequence: You wrestle the window down and wedge a magazine under it, and notice the latch was already fastened, and decide firmly not to think about the latch.
You pull the quilt up to her chin and tell yourself old houses breathe. She sleeps through the rest of it. You do not.

nodes.text: She found the board in the basement with the summer furniture, and she plays it by herself, which is not how the game is meant to work. Over cereal she explains Captain Howdy: he answers the questions she only thinks, and he is not always nice about it. She does his voice for you. It is an ordinary twelve-year-old doing a funny voice, right up until it isn't.

choices.consequence: You ask three careful questions across the breakfast table and get three cheerful answers, and cheerfulness turns out not to be the reassurance you wanted.
You laugh, because it is a child with an imaginary friend, and the laugh is entirely genuine, and you will be replaying it for years.

nodes.text: The steps drop from Prospect Street down to M in one straight flight, walled both sides, wet all year with whatever the brick holds onto. People use them as a shortcut and curse them in ice. Regan's bedroom window sits at the top of them, three feet back from the edge. You have walked past this staircase daily for a month without ever once looking up at your own house.

choices.consequence: You go by with your collar up and your mind on a phone call, and the steps drop away behind you into their own private weather.
You stand at the bottom counting windows until you find hers — lit, curtain still. It is a foolish thing to be doing, and you keep doing it.

nodes.text: The ward smells of ammonia and boiled vegetables, and the woman in the bed is very small under the sheet and speaking Greek at you, because English is for other people. She wants to know why you left her here. You are a Jesuit and a psychiatrist, the Church takes your salary, and there is no money anywhere for a private room. Someone across the aisle is arguing with a television that is switched off.

choices.consequence: You ride the subway uptown on your day off and sit holding her hand, and she asks again why you left, and you have no better answer than last week's.
You have three counselling hours, a lecture, and a perfectly decent excuse, and you use the excuse, and you will pay interest on that one Sunday forever.

nodes.text: A dozen guests, a piano, and Burke Dennings holding court with a drink in either hand. Regan comes down the staircase in her nightgown, barefoot, and halts in the middle of the rug. She looks at the astronaut in the corner and tells him, pleasantly, that he is going to die up there. Then she urinates on the carpet and goes on standing in it, entirely calm.

choices.consequence: You laugh it off, say she walks in her sleep, hand her to the housekeeper — and the party has moved on to another subject inside ninety seconds.
You get her upstairs fast with a hand between her shoulder blades, and behind you the room carries on being a party, and that is the part you keep.

nodes.text: Twelve specialists in four weeks. They X-ray her skull, run the EEG, put a needle into her spine twice, and every result comes back within normal limits. One of them says hysteria. Another suggests Ritalin and a rest. She is thrashing hard enough to bruise both arms on the bedframe and she has bitten a nurse through the glove. The last doctor mentions, awkwardly, that there exists a ritual.

choices.consequence: You take her to a fourth hospital and sit in the waiting room with the folder on your knees, and the folder is now thicker than the phone book.
You stop asking for tests and start asking what happens next, which is the moment medicine formally hands your child back to you.

nodes.text: They find the director at the foot of the M Street steps with his head turned most of the way round. He had been sitting with her while you were out — an hour, less. The housekeeper heard nothing at all. The police say a fall, then say a fall does not usually do that to a neck. Upstairs, the bedroom window stands open. It has been shut and latched all week.

choices.consequence: You raise your eyes the whole flight to a lit square with a curtain shifting in it, and something inside you closes over like a door in a draft.
You keep your eyes on the wet pavement and answer the officer's questions in order, and the not-looking costs you more than looking would have.

nodes.text: He turns up apologetic, a heavy man in a bad coat with a story about his daughter wanting an autograph. He circles for twenty minutes — the picture, the weather, a film he saw twice — and then asks, mildly, whether anyone could have reached that window. He mentions the desecrations at the church down the hill. Throughout, he is watching your hands rather than your face.

choices.consequence: You give him the truth about the window and watch him write none of it down, and understand he knew already and came to see what you would do with it.
You say the window sticks, the house is old, the child is ill. He accepts every word kindly and leaves you alone with everything you left out.

nodes.text: You go up because she is calling for you, and the bedroom door is warm on the hallway side and cold on the other. She is on her back with her spine arched, and the bed lifts — frame, mattress, springs together — and hangs three feet clear of the floorboards with the sheets still tucked at the corners. It is not sudden. It is careful, like a jack under a car.

choices.consequence: You cross the room and take her fingers while the bed is still up in the air, because she is under all of that somewhere, and you say her name twice.
You put your back to the wardrobe and stay there, and later you will never be able to explain the arithmetic that held you against that wall.

nodes.text: You are stripping the bed and your hand goes under the pillow and closes on it. A small brass crucifix on a chain, the sort a nurse might wear, and nobody in this house is Catholic and nobody in this house owns one. It is about the length of a spoon. You stand there doing arithmetic about a twelve-year-old and a locked room, and then you make yourself stop doing it.

choices.consequence: You put it in your coat pocket and it stays there for weeks, warming against your ribs, and you never once take it out to look at it again.
You slide it back under the pillow at the precise angle you found it, smooth the case flat, and go downstairs and pour a drink you do not finish.

nodes.text: The Jesuit brings a reel-to-reel and runs her voice backwards through it at your kitchen table, at normal volume, with the percolator going. Forwards it is animal noise. Backwards there are words — English, in the wrong order but not wrong enough. Let her die. A name. Something frightened. He plays it three times through, and the tape hiss in the gaps between phrases is the part that gets you.

choices.consequence: You sit through all three passes with both palms flat on the table, and afterwards every ordinary noise in the house carries a possible second meaning.
You reach across and lift the head off the tape, and the silence in the kitchen is no improvement, and you cannot unhear what you already heard.

nodes.text: A boxer's face, a black coat, and a doubt he carries around like a limp. He has come as a psychiatrist; he wants to discuss seizures and suggestibility, and he mentions that the Church has not authorised an exorcism in this country since before the war. You take his coat and hang it. Upstairs, a voice starts using his dead mother's exact Greek, asking why he left her there.

choices.consequence: You hang the coat and offer coffee as though this were any evening visit, and the ordinary manners hold the house upright for about four more minutes.
You catch his sleeve on the landing and ask him outright, and a man who has stopped believing in anything looks at you and does not say no.

nodes.text: He fills an empty Coke bottle at your kitchen tap, blesses it in the doorway, and carries it up as a test, because he expects nothing and intends to prove it. He shakes it over the bed. Her forearm reddens and rises into welts as fast as a kettle scald and she screams in a register that empties his face. Afterwards he tells you, quietly, that he never blessed the water at all.

choices.consequence: You write down the time and what was actually in the bottle, because somebody in this house has to keep a record that a tribunal would accept.
You shake it over her again to be sure, and get an identical result twice, and being sure provides no comfort of any kind.

nodes.text: The room is at forty degrees and smells like a hospital crossed with a barn. She stops mid-word, her stomach draws in hard, and letters push up under the skin from beneath — raised, pink, legible clear across the width of her. Three syllables you have never heard in your life, and which an old man on a hill outside Mosul would read at a glance. Then the skin goes flat again.

choices.consequence: You fetch the camera from the hall table and take two frames with the flash, and the prints come back from the drugstore perfectly, uselessly clear.
You draw the sheet up over her stomach before the priest turns round, as though modesty were still one of the things at stake in this room.

nodes.text: A taxi at the kerb in the rain, and an old man gets out with a black bag and a hat and then does not come in. He stands on the wet pavement looking up at the lit window for a long moment, the way a man looks at a job he has done once before and did not walk away from cleanly. Inside, the house says his name down the stairs before he rings.

choices.consequence: You stand aside and let the old man take the staircase first, and being relieved of the decision feels almost indistinguishable from being forgiven.
You start in on the medical history in the hallway and he lifts one hand, gently, and says there is only one entity up there, and that it lies.

nodes.text: Two priests on a landing with cold air coming under the door in a visible line along the boards. Merrin puts on the purple stole, hands you the book, and tells you not to converse with it — not once, whatever voice it borrows. He asks whether you are ready. Behind the door something says both your names in both your mothers' voices, one after the other, then waits politely for an answer.

choices.consequence: You knock at a door inside a house you were invited into, twice, like a guest, and whatever is on the other side finds that funny for a long moment.
You go in shoulder-first without pausing, and the cold hits you like standing water, and your first breath in that room comes out white.

nodes.text: The rite is Latin and repetitive on purpose. The bed jumps clear of the floor. The wardrobe walks a foot sideways. It calls Merrin by a name he last heard in an African village decades ago, then starts in on you: your mother's ward, the smell of the corridor, the Sunday you did not go. The window glass cracks inward along one long line. Merrin does not alter his pace by a syllable.

choices.consequence: You keep your thumb in the page and read the responses straight over the top of the voice, and the reading is the only floor left underneath you.
You stop for one breath and it fills the gap instantly with something true about you, and now you understand why he said not to converse.

nodes.text: You went down for fresh water. You come back to a quiet room and the old man kneeling at the bedside, not praying. His face is the colour of wet newspaper, the pill bottle is open on the rug with tablets scattered into the pile, and the girl is asleep or something adjacent to it. He has one hand flat on the mattress, and he is no longer using it to hold himself up.

choices.consequence: You lift the stole off a dead man's shoulders and put it over your own, which is the first thing you have done in a year without hesitating first.
You kneel and start the prayer for the dying and get four words in before the voice in the bed joins you, in perfect time, word for word.

nodes.text: You hit it. You hit a twelve-year-old's body with a closed fist and it laughs up at you through her split lip, and you haul it upright by the pyjama front and say it: take me instead, come into me. You keep saying it. The pressure in the room shifts the way weather shifts, and your own reflection in the black window above the bed is not doing what you are doing.

choices.consequence: You issue the invitation out loud three times, and it accepts with the eagerness of something that has been waiting all month for exactly that offer.
You get an arm across his chest and he goes straight through it, and you realise this was settled years ago in a hospital ward uptown.

nodes.text: You have about four seconds of your own hands left and you know it. The girl is on the floor behind you, breathing, hers again, one shoe off. The sash is up. The whole flight goes down from that sill to M Street and the brick has a wet shine on it. Someone is running up the stairs. The thing inside you is already reaching for the child, using your arm to do it.

choices.consequence: You throw your own body at the open frame while the arm is still arguing with you, and the last decision you ever make, you make very fast.
You hold on one extra second to be certain it is really in you, and that second is charity, and it nearly costs the girl everything.
You think instead of a green stone figure in a crate in a seminary basement, and of how far a thing can travel inside a shipping manifest.

nodes.text: She wakes asking for pancakes and cannot say why the room is cold or why both her arms hurt. She remembers a dog with a long snout, she says, and after that nothing. In the hallway she stops in front of a priest's white collar and kisses his cheek without being able to explain the impulse, and you stand among the suitcases while the movers carry the bed out, and you do not correct her.

Dyer comes down the flight two at a time and kneels on wet brick and asks him whether he is sorry, and gets a squeeze of the hand for yes, and gives absolution to a man who cannot say a word of it. Above them, a curtain moves in a lit window. In the morning the city runs a short item on an inside page about a Jesuit who fell, filed beside the weather.

The amulet goes back into a crate, back onto a ship, back up a hill outside Mosul, where a young archaeologist puts it into the ground at the level it came from and marks the spot on no chart anywhere. Wind comes over it in the afternoons and takes the sand off and puts it back. For one entire summer nobody in that valley dreams badly, and nobody notices, which is what a quiet summer is.
